desc: Three consecutive front-page articles by Ansel E. Talbert, Military and Aviation Editor of the New York Herald Tribune, published 20, 21 and 22 November 1955 under the titles 'Conquest of Gravity Aim Of Top Scientists in U. S.', 'Space-Ship Marvel Seen If Gravity Is Outwitted' and 'New Air Dream, Planes Flying Outside Gravity'. They are the contemporaneous press record behind every later claim that American aerospace executives said on the record in the 1950s that gravity could be controlled. They name the firms, quote Lawrence D. Bell, William P. Lear and George S. Trimble jr. directly, and report the founding of the Chapel Hill gravity institute under an earlier name. They do not mention Thomas Townsend Brown.

dossier.narrative: This series is the load-bearing document under a whole branch of the electrogravitics literature, and reading it moves four things at once. It dates the reporting to November 1955 rather than 1953. It gives George Trimble his actual office, vice-president in charge of advanced design planning of Martin Aircraft, rather than chief executive, and shows that his atom-bomb comparison is about the time the bomb took and not about the money it cost. It names the Sperry Gyroscope Division of Sperry-Rand among the firms with scientists on the gravity problem, which is the documented attachment for a node the 30 August pass left deliberately unattached. And it reports the University of North Carolina trustees approving a gravity institute earlier that month under the name Institute of Pure Physics, with Gordon Gray's approval, Agnew H. Bahnson jr. as fundraiser and the directorship offered to Bryce S. DeWitt, which is the Institute of Field Physics before it had its final name. What it does not contain is the figure the electrogravitics claim usually rests on: Thomas Townsend Brown is named in none of the three articles, and neither Winterhaven nor any Navy or Air Force electrogravitics contract appears in them. That absence is carried here as a claim and deliberately not as an edge.
openQuestions: Whether the Herald Tribune ran any follow-up or correction to the series.
What the 'Institute of Pure Physics' name change to Institute of Field Physics turned on, which the series does not say.
